stem: A policy states that contractors may open design documents only from a managed device, during business hours, and while inside the country. Which access control model is this?

options.why: The decision combines several attributes at once: employment type, device state, time and location. That combination is ABAC.
RBAC decides on job function alone. It cannot express device posture, time of day and location together.
MAC decides by security labels and clearances assigned centrally, which is not what is described.
DAC leaves the decision to the resource owner. Here a central policy decides.

stem: On a file server, the creator of a folder can grant other users access to it at their own discretion. Which model is in use?

options.why: The owner of the resource decides who may access it. That discretion is the defining feature.
Under MAC the system enforces labels and users cannot override them, which is the opposite of owner discretion.
RBAC assigns access by job function, administered centrally, not granted ad hoc by whoever made the folder.
Rule-based applies global conditions to everyone, such as a time restriction, regardless of owner.

stem: An accounts payable clerk can both create a new supplier record and approve payments to it. Which principle is violated?

options.why: One person can complete an entire sensitive transaction alone, which is the fraud scenario separation of duties exists to prevent.
Least privilege is arguably implicated, and the precise principle is that a single process must be split between people.
Need to know restricts which data you may see. The problem here is which actions one person may complete.
Job rotation limits how long one person holds a role. It does not address combining two duties today.

stem: An analyst is cleared to access case files but is found browsing cases unrelated to any assignment. Which principle should be enforced?

options.why: Clearance establishes that they may handle this class of data. Need to know restricts them to the specific records their work requires.
Least privilege concerns the permissions and actions granted. Here the permission level is correct and the data scope is not.
No single process is being completed by one person. Nothing about duties is at issue.
A detective control for long running fraud, unrelated to scoping data access.

stem: A data centre is valued at 2,000,000. A flood would destroy 25% of it, and floods are expected once every four years. What is the ALE?

options.why: SLE is 2,000,000 times 0.25, which is 500,000. ARO for once in four years is 0.25. ALE is 500,000 times 0.25, which is 125,000.
That is the SLE, the cost of one event. ALE is the annualised figure, so it must be multiplied by the ARO.
That is the asset value. The exposure factor of 25% has not been applied.
Treating once in four years as an ARO of 4 rather than 0.25 inverts the rate and inflates the result enormously.

stem: A control costing 40,000 per year would eliminate a risk with an ALE of 25,000. What does quantitative analysis suggest?

options.text: Do not buy the control; it costs more than the loss it prevents
options.why: Spending 40,000 a year to avoid 25,000 a year of expected loss destroys value. The organisation would accept or otherwise treat the risk.

options.text: Buy the control, because eliminating risk always justifies the cost
options.why: Risk management is economic. A control that costs more than the exposure is not justified on those grounds.

options.text: Buy the control, because the SLE will exceed 40,000
options.why: The SLE is not given, and the annualised comparison is the relevant one for an annual cost.

options.text: Recalculate, since ALE cannot be lower than the control cost
options.why: There is no such constraint. ALE frequently comes out below the cost of eliminating it.

stem: A business impact analysis states that the order system may lose no more than 15 minutes of transactions. Which metric is this, and what does it drive?

options.text: RPO, which sets the backup or replication frequency
options.why: RPO looks backwards from the outage and defines acceptable data loss, so backups must run at least that often.

options.text: RTO, which sets how quickly service must be restored
options.why: RTO looks forwards and concerns downtime. This statement is about lost data, not elapsed time.

options.text: MTTR, which measures average repair time
options.why: MTTR is an observed measurement of repairs, not a target set by the business.

options.text: MTBF, which measures time between failures
options.why: MTBF describes reliability across an asset's life and says nothing about acceptable data loss.

stem: Which pair correctly separates a target the business sets from a metric the organisation observes?

options.text: RTO is a target; MTTR is an observed measurement
options.why: RTO is chosen by the business as the maximum tolerable downtime. MTTR is measured from actual repairs.

options.text: MTTR is a target; RTO is an observed measurement
options.why: Reversed. You do not observe an RTO, you commit to it.

options.text: RPO and RTO are both observed measurements
options.why: Both are targets set in the business impact analysis.

options.text: MTBF is a target; RPO is an observed measurement
options.why: Both are reversed. MTBF is measured, RPO is set.

stem: A board resolution states the organisation will pursue aggressive growth into new markets and accepts elevated risk in doing so. Which term does this describe?

options.why: Risk appetite is the strategic level of risk an organisation is willing to take to pursue its objectives, and expansionary is one of the three named stances.
Tolerance is the acceptable variation around the appetite, set by management per risk, not the board level strategic stance.
A threshold is the specific trip wire recorded in the risk register that triggers action.
Transference is a treatment strategy, such as insurance. This statement sets a posture, not a treatment.

stem: Where are individual risks, their owners, their current scores and the levels that trigger escalation recorded?

options.why: The register is the working record of identified risks, owners, key risk indicators and thresholds.
The appetite statement sets the overall posture. It does not track individual risks.
The BIA determines the impact of disruption to processes and produces RTO and RPO figures.
That documents which controls apply and why, not the risks themselves.

stem: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical finding on a server. Investigation confirms the patch was applied two weeks ago and the vulnerability is not present. What is this?

options.why: The tool raised an alarm and there was nothing there. Positive means the tool reported something, false means it was wrong.
A false negative is silence in the presence of a real problem. Here the tool spoke up.

options.text: A true positive that needs revalidation
options.why: A true positive is a real finding. This was confirmed not to be present.
A true negative is correct silence. The scanner did not stay silent.

stem: Which outcome is the most dangerous for a detection system, and why?

options.text: A false negative, because a real attack goes unreported
options.why: Nobody is alerted and nobody investigates. The organisation believes it is safe while it is not.

options.text: A false positive, because analysts waste time
options.why: Costly and corrosive through alert fatigue, and still not the outcome that lets an attacker operate undetected.

options.text: A true positive, because it means an attack succeeded
options.why: A true positive means the system worked. Detection is not the same as compromise.

options.text: A true negative, because nothing is logged
options.why: A true negative is correct silence when there is genuinely nothing to report.

stem: A retailer must validate its disaster recovery plan before the holiday season without any impact on production. Which test is appropriate?

options.why: Participants talk through the plan in a room. It has no production impact, which the requirement demands.

options.text: A full failover test to the recovery site
options.why: The most conclusive test and the most disruptive. The stem forbids production impact.
Lower impact than failover and still brings up recovery systems alongside production, so it is not zero impact.

options.text: A simulation with systems partially engaged
options.why: Simulations touch systems and carry some risk. Discussion only means tabletop.

stem: Which test provides the strongest evidence that the recovery site can genuinely carry production load?

options.text: A full failover test with production cut over to the recovery site
options.why: Only actually running production at the recovery site proves it can. Everything else is inference.

options.text: A tabletop exercise attended by all system owners
options.why: Discussion validates the plan on paper and proves nothing about the systems.

options.text: A walkthrough of the runbooks with the operations team
options.why: A walkthrough checks the procedure is complete and correct, not that the infrastructure works.

options.text: Reviewing the recovery site's capacity documentation
options.why: Documentation review is the weakest form of assurance available.

stem: An employee receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the IT service desk, asking them to read out the code that just arrived on their phone. What is this?

options.why: The channel is a voice call, which makes it vishing, and the goal is to defeat the second factor.
Technically part of the phishing family, and the exam wants the channel specific term when the channel is stated.
Smishing arrives by SMS. The code arrived by SMS, the attack arrived by phone call.
Whaling targets an executive. Nothing indicates the employee is one.

stem: Finance receives an email from the CFO's genuine mailbox, in their usual style, asking for an urgent wire transfer to a new account. Mail authentication passes because the message really did come from that mailbox. What is this?

options.why: The attacker controls a real, legitimate mailbox, which is why SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass and the message reads as authentic.
Whaling targets an executive. Here the executive's account is the weapon, and finance staff are the target.
Nothing is spoofed. The message genuinely originates from the CFO's account, which is what makes it so effective.
The channel is email, not SMS.

stem: Authentication logs show a single failed sign-in against each of 340 different accounts over two hours, from one source. No accounts locked out. What is happening?

options.why: One common password tried against many accounts, deliberately staying under the lockout threshold. Wide and shallow is the signature.
Brute force concentrates many attempts on one account, which produces a large failure count and a lockout.
Stuffing uses leaked username and password pairs and typically produces a mix of successes and failures.

options.text: A denial of service attempt against the directory
options.why: 340 attempts over two hours is negligible load. The pattern is reconnaissance for valid credentials.

stem: Why does an account lockout policy fail to stop password spraying?

options.text: The attack deliberately stays below the lockout threshold on every account
options.why: Spraying exists precisely to evade lockout. One or two attempts per account never reaches the limit, so MFA and impossible travel detection are the real answers.

options.text: Lockout policies only apply to administrative accounts
options.why: Lockout applies to whatever accounts it is configured for, typically all of them.

options.text: Spraying uses valid credentials, so nothing fails
options.why: That describes credential stuffing with known-good pairs. Spraying is guessing, and most attempts fail.

options.text: Lockout counters reset only at midnight
options.why: Reset windows vary and are not the reason. The attack simply never reaches the threshold.

stem: A web application concatenates a user supplied search term directly into a database query. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Use parameterised queries so input is never treated as code
options.why: Parameterisation separates the query structure from the data, which removes the class of vulnerability rather than filtering symptoms.

options.text: Apply input validation to reject suspicious characters
options.why: Worth doing as defence in depth, and filters are routinely bypassed. Parameterisation is the structural fix.

options.text: HTML encode the search term before displaying it
options.why: Output encoding defends against cross site scripting. It does nothing about the query sent to the database.

options.text: Set the HttpOnly flag on the session cookie
options.why: HttpOnly limits the damage of cross site scripting. It is unrelated to SQL injection.

stem: An attacker stores a script in a forum post. When other users view the thread, their session cookies are sent to the attacker's server. What is the attack, and who is the victim?

options.text: Stored cross site scripting; the victims are the other users viewing the page
options.why: The payload executes in each visitor's browser under the site's origin, which is why it can read their session.

options.text: SQL injection; the victim is the database
options.why: Nothing is being interpreted by the database. The payload runs in a browser.

options.text: Cross site request forgery; the victim is the forum server
options.why: CSRF makes a victim's browser perform an action, it does not execute attacker script to steal cookies.

options.text: Directory traversal; the victims are other users
options.why: Traversal reads files outside the intended path on the server. No script runs in anyone's browser.
